prompt: In the output of `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe`, what is `LAG` for one partition?

choices.text: The seconds since the group last committed
choices.why: Lag here is a count of messages, not a duration.

choices.text: LOG-END-OFFSET minus CURRENT-OFFSET
choices.why: Right: written and not yet handled by the group.

choices.text: The number of members the group is missing
choices.why: Members are not counted in that column at all.

choices.text: The messages the broker has not yet copied to disk
choices.why: Lag is about a reader's position, not about the broker's writes.

prompt: Producers write 20 sales a second and the consumer handles 10. Roughly how does the lag change while the tills are running?

choices.text: It stays flat at the first value it reached
choices.why: It would stay flat only if the two rates were equal.

choices.text: It grows by about 30 a second, the sum of both rates
choices.why: The consumer's reading takes messages away; the rates are subtracted.

choices.text: It grows by about 10 a second
choices.why: Right: twenty in, ten out.

choices.text: It grows until the consumer crashes from the load
choices.why: A pulling consumer is never sent more than it asks for; it falls behind, it does not crash.

prompt: A consumer works through sales correctly but never commits its offsets. What does `--describe` show for its group while it works?

choices.text: A lag that never goes down
choices.why: Right: the tool measures from the committed position, which never moves.

choices.text: A lag of zero, since every sale was handled
choices.why: The tool cannot see what the program handled, only what it committed.

choices.text: An error saying the group does not exist
choices.why: The group exists while it has a member; its committed offsets are just absent.

choices.text: The same lag as a group that commits, a second later
choices.why: Without commits there is nothing for the lag to follow.

prompt: The number of messages written to a partition and not yet handled by a group is called consumer ___.
Two topics each show a lag of 1000 messages. One receives 1000 sales a second, the other one sale a minute. What does that tell you?

choices.text: Both are equally far behind
choices.why: Equal counts, very different ages: one second against about seventeen hours.

choices.text: The busy topic is in more trouble, because it has more traffic
choices.why: Its lag is one second old; the quiet one's is from yesterday.

choices.text: Neither can be judged until their lag is turned into a time
choices.why: The rates in the question already turn it into time; that is the point.

choices.text: The quiet topic's consumer is hours behind
choices.why: Right: about seventeen hours, against one second.

prompt: How does `lag_seconds.py` find how long the oldest unhandled message has waited?

choices.text: It subtracts the waiting message's timestamp from now
choices.why: Right: that message is the oldest one waiting.

choices.text: It divides the lag by the producer's rate
choices.why: That estimates the time to drain; the program reads a timestamp instead.

choices.text: It reads the `at` field the tills put inside each sale
choices.why: It uses the record's own timestamp, which the producer set.

choices.text: It joins the group and times its own poll
choices.why: It deliberately never joins, so it does not cause a rebalance.

prompt: A group has a lag of 600 messages and its consumer handles 15 a second. If nothing else arrives, how many seconds does it need to catch up?
Why does `lag_seconds.py` create one consumer with the group's id that never subscribes?

choices.text: To take over the partitions while the measurement runs
choices.why: Taking them over would stop the real members; it avoids exactly that.

choices.text: To read the group's offsets without joining
choices.why: Right: joining would rebalance the group being measured.

choices.text: Because Kafka refuses to read a message without a group
choices.why: The reading is done by the other consumer, under a group of its own.

choices.text: So the measurement commits for the group
choices.why: Auto commit is off, and it never commits anything.

prompt: Why does a slow Kafka consumer not need to push back on the producer?

choices.text: Because the broker slows the producer down automatically
choices.why: The producer is not slowed: the tills finished on time.

choices.text: Consumers pull, and the log on disk holds the backlog
choices.why: Right: the log is the buffer, and lag is how full it is.

choices.text: Because messages a consumer cannot keep up with are dropped
choices.why: Nothing is dropped; they wait in the log.

choices.text: The producer waits for each consumer's reply
choices.why: Producers and consumers never talk to each other directly.

prompt: A consumer with `max.poll.interval.ms` of 6000 spends 8 seconds on one sale. What happens at six seconds?

choices.text: The broker deletes the sale
choices.why: Nothing is deleted; the member's position is what is at stake.

choices.text: Its heartbeat thread stops and the session times out
choices.why: Heartbeats keep going from the client's own thread; the poll interval is a separate clock.

choices.text: The member leaves the group and its partitions are reassigned
choices.why: Right: presumed stuck, it is removed, which is a rebalance.

choices.text: Nothing, because the limit is only checked when it polls
choices.why: The client checks it on its own and leaves; the program learns at its next poll.

prompt: In the `audit` group, the member that took half a second per sale kept being revoked and assigned. Why did it suffer for the other member's slowness?

choices.text: Its own processing was also too slow for the limit
choices.why: Half a second is well inside six seconds.

choices.text: The two shared a single thread in one process
choices.why: They ran in different shells, as different processes.

choices.text: Its partitions were full of poison messages
choices.why: There was no bad message in this demonstration.

choices.text: Each leave and rejoin rebalances the whole group
choices.why: Right: a rebalance is the group's, not one member's.

prompt: Match each fix for the poll-interval loop to what it changes.

pairs.right: the limit the work is measured against
how much work one poll hands over
polling continues while the work runs

right_distractors: the number of brokers in the cluster

prompt: A consumer throws on one record, restarts, and throws on it again. What has stopped?

choices.text: Every topic on the cluster
choices.why: Other readers and other topics carry on.

choices.text: Only the sales with the bad record's key
choices.why: Every key that shares the partition waits behind it, not just its own.

choices.text: Its progress through that partition
choices.why: Right: its position cannot move past the record it fails on.

choices.text: The producer, until the record is removed
choices.why: Producers keep writing; the backlog grows behind the bad record.

prompt: What does `sturdy_consumer.py` put in the headers of a dead letter?

choices.text: The error, and the topic, partition and offset it came from
choices.why: Right: enough to find it, understand it and send it back.

choices.text: The corrected sale
choices.why: It copies the original value as it was; nothing is corrected.

choices.text: The group's committed offset
choices.why: The origin is the bad message's own position, not the group's.

choices.text: A retry counter
choices.why: This program does not retry; the headers are the error and the origin.

prompt: The stock consumer fails because the database it writes to is down for two seconds. Should that message go to the dead-letter topic?

choices.text: Yes, every failure goes there, so the partition keeps moving
choices.why: Then an ordinary sale is set aside for a problem that has already passed.

choices.text: No: retry it, since the failure is transient
choices.why: Right: dead letters are for what fails the same way every time.

choices.text: Yes, and the database should be restarted
choices.why: The message itself is fine; nothing about it needs setting aside.

choices.text: No, it should be deleted from the topic
choices.why: Nothing deletes a single message from a topic, and nothing is wrong with it.

prompt: The counter is stuck on a bad message, the only one in partition 2, and `--describe` shows lag 0 on every partition it lists. Why does the lag not show the problem?

choices.text: The bad message was deleted by the broker
choices.why: It is still there; the next run meets it again.

choices.text: Lag is counted only for keys that parse as JSON
choices.why: Lag knows nothing about what a message contains.

choices.text: The group never committed in partition 2, and lag is measured from commits
choices.why: Right: with no commit there, the tool has nothing to print for it.

choices.text: The consumer had already handled it
choices.why: It crashed on it, twice; nothing was handled.

prompt: A topic where a consumer copies the messages it cannot handle, with the reason, is called a dead-___ topic.
Why did `--reset-offsets --execute` refuse to move the group `stock`?

choices.text: The topic had no messages left to replay
choices.why: The 600 sales were all there.

choices.text: A member was still running
choices.why: Right: the group was Stable, and its member would overwrite the reset.

choices.text: `--to-earliest` is only allowed with `--dry-run`
choices.why: It works with `--execute` once the group is inactive.

choices.text: Resetting needs a cluster of three nodes
choices.why: The reset ran on one node a moment later.

prompt: A reset `--to-datetime` is given 09:00 on Monday. Which time does it compare with?

choices.text: The time inside each message, the `at` field
choices.why: The broker knows nothing about fields inside the value.

choices.text: The time the group last committed
choices.why: Commit times are not what the reset searches.

choices.text: The time each record was written, its record timestamp
choices.why: Right: it asks the broker for offsets by record timestamp.

choices.text: The time the segment file was created
choices.why: The lookup is per record, through the time index.

prompt: The stock consumer adds each sale's quantity to a running total in a database. What happens if you replay last week without changing it?

choices.text: Those days' sales are counted twice
choices.why: Right: replay is at-least-once on purpose; the consumer must set, not add.

choices.text: The totals are corrected, because the new run replaces the old
choices.why: Adding does not replace; that is what an idempotent write would do.

choices.text: Kafka refuses to deliver messages a group has already read
choices.why: Delivering them again is exactly what the reset asked for.

choices.text: Nothing, since the database notices
choices.why: The database sees ordinary additions; nothing tells it they are repeats.

prompt: Put the steps of a careful replay in order.
items: Fix the consumer and make it safe to run twice
Stop every member of the group
Run the reset as a dry run

prompt: In blue-green reprocessing, why does the new version get its own `group.id`?

choices.text: Kafka allows one program per group
choices.why: A group can have many members running the same program; that is not the reason.

choices.text: To start from the oldest message, old group untouched
choices.why: Right: new group, no committed offsets, the old one untouched.

choices.text: So that it reads faster
choices.why: Speed comes from instances and partitions, not from the name.

choices.text: To write to a different topic
choices.why: The output topic is a separate choice; the group decides where reading starts.

prompt: After `stock-v2` read the whole topic, `sales.dlq` held the bad sale twice. What does that show?

choices.text: The dead-letter producer has a bug
choices.why: It did what it was told, once per version.

choices.text: The old group was not deleted in time
choices.why: Deleting the group removes offsets; it does not stop the new version's writes.

choices.text: A side effect happens again when a new version reprocesses
choices.why: Right: anything written outside the group's own output repeats.

choices.text: Kafka duplicated a message on disk
choices.why: Two writes produced two messages; nothing was duplicated by the broker.

prompt: What does `kafka-topics.sh --describe --under-replicated-partitions` print on a healthy cluster?

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right: an empty list is the healthy answer.

choices.text: Every partition, with its leader
choices.why: That is plain `--describe`; the option filters to the problem cases.

choices.text: The word OK
choices.why: It prints partitions or nothing; there is no status word.

choices.text: The partitions with no leader
choices.why: Those are `--unavailable-partitions`.

prompt: Why is "lag above 1000" a poor alert for the stock consumer?

choices.text: Lag cannot go above 1000 on a topic with three partitions
choices.why: Nothing caps lag except retention.

choices.text: Kafka resets the lag every hour
choices.why: Lag only falls when the consumer reads.

choices.text: It needs a metrics system that does not exist
choices.why: The number is easy to collect; the trouble is what it means.

choices.text: It fires at every busy peak that drains on its own
choices.why: Right: alert on lag in time and on sustained growth instead.

prompt: A consumer crashed at 01:00 and no sales arrive until 09:00. Which alert fires first?

choices.text: Lag growing for fifteen minutes
choices.why: With no sales, the lag does not grow until nine.

choices.text: A group with no members
choices.why: Right: the absence is visible at once, traffic or not.

choices.text: Under-replicated partitions
choices.why: The brokers are fine; only a consumer stopped.

choices.text: Free disk on a log volume
choices.why: Nothing is being written, so the disk does not change.

prompt: Which of these deserve an alarm that wakes somebody? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: An offline partition
choices.why: Yes: writes and reads to it are failing now.

choices.text: Lag in time above what the output promises
choices.why: Yes: the promise is already broken.

choices.text: Bytes in per second higher than yesterday
choices.why: That is a dashboard number; nobody has to act on it.

choices.text: A rebalance when a consumer is deployed
choices.why: Deploys rebalance by design.

choices.text: Free space running out on a log volume
choices.why: Yes: a full disk stops writes and does not recover by itself.

prompt: Monday 10:00: the stock page is three hours stale, the lag of `stock` has grown all morning, and its consumer prints a `MAXPOLL` warning every few seconds. What is the first thing to look at?

choices.text: Why one record takes longer than the poll interval
choices.why: Right: that loop is the cause; the lag is the symptom.

choices.text: Whether the topic has enough retention
choices.why: Retention decides how far back you can replay, not why the consumer is slow.

choices.text: Reset the group to the latest offset
choices.why: That hides the lag by skipping three hours of stock changes.

choices.text: Add brokers to the cluster
choices.why: The brokers are not the slow part; the consumer is.

prompt: Put the blue-green reprocessing steps in order.
items: Start the new version under a new group, writing to its own output
Wait until its lag reaches zero
Compare its output with the old one
Switch the readers to the new output

prompt: A dead-letter topic has received 40 messages since Friday and nobody has looked. What has the platform effectively done with those 40 sales?

choices.text: Processed them later, automatically
choices.why: Nothing reads a dead-letter topic unless somebody makes it.

choices.text: Dropped them, more slowly
choices.why: Right: a dead-letter topic nobody reads is a slower way of losing data.

choices.text: Kept them in order with the other sales
choices.why: Moving a message aside gives up its order.

choices.text: Retried each one until it succeeded
choices.why: The consumer moved on; nothing retries dead letters.
